  to replay TinyLFU/ARC2/LRU and the new method.
runpod_compute_profile: cpu_heavy
ideal_dataset_criteria: >-
  The ideal dataset pairs a REAL request trace (item IDs, ordered request sequence, timestamps, per-item request counts showing
  Zipf/heavy-skew popularity) with REAL images so that CLIP embeddings and semantic clusters are genuine and reproducible.
  Concretely: 1,000–20,000 unique items per regime with ~100k–1M total requests; each item carries a 512-d CLIP (ViT-B/32)
  embedding, a semantic cluster id, and its true popularity (request count); PLUS the full ordered request sequence is retained
  (not collapsed to aggregates) so the experiment can replay TinyLFU/ARC2/LRU/bandit/Chameleon policies and compute hit/miss.
  Total footprint under ~300MB. Three regimes with distinct dynamics. Folds split by timestamp (temporal order preserved,
  no future leakage). The dataset must be raw data ONLY: NO hit/miss labels, conformal intervals, or admission decisions should
  be computed here — those are downstream experiment/derived outputs.
dataset_search_plan: |-
  CRITICAL CORRECTION TO THE DIRECTION: (1) OpenRouter does NOT expose CLIP/image-embedding endpoints — it is a text-LLM gateway. Extract embeddings LOCALLY instead using open_clip_torch (ViT-B/32, 512-d) or transformers.CLIPModel on CPU; this also means the $10 OpenRouter budget is not needed for this artifact. (2) Real cache traces (Tencent photo CDN, Microsoft, Wikipedia, SNIA IOTTA block traces) ship item IDs + request sequences + counts but NOT the image bytes, so visual embeddings cannot come from the trace itself — the access pattern and the images must come from two real sources and be paired procedurally.

  PHASE A — Acquire real access-pattern ground truth: Search HuggingFace and GitHub for public cache/CDN trace datasets. Named candidates to check: (a) the Caffeine simulator traces (github.com/ben-manes/caffeine/wiki/Simulator, Traces section) which reference the Tencent photo CDN, Microsoft, Wikipedia, Gloe/S3/UMass traces; (b) the pennshen trace repos on GitHub (LC/CacheLib-traces / PBC) hosting large CDN traces; (c) SNIA IOTTA block-I/O repository (iotta.snia.org). Use aii-hf-datasets search (queries: 'cache trace', 'cdn access log', 'web trace', 'request trace') and aii-web-tools search as fallback. Goal: an ordered request stream + per-item request counts that exhibit heavy-tailed popularity. If no directly loadable trace is found, RECORD the trace's Zipf/skew statistics and request-count distribution and use them as the ground-truth generator for the request sequences (still real-derived, not fabricated ab initio).

  PHASE B — Acquire real images: Use aii-hf-datasets to pull a loadable image corpus — ImageNet-1k subset (via timm/HF mirror) or COCO (e.g. a HF coco/ image subset) is preferred for real semantic clusters (animals, vehicles, food, scenes). Target a few thousand down to 20k images. Confirm 'loadable=True' before choosing.

  PHASE C — Pair and embed: Assign each trace item to a real image deterministically (seeded), cluster items by image class/label into a 'cluster_id' column. Extract 512-d CLIP embeddings locally (CLIP ViT-B/32, CPU-batch, float32→float16 if needed for size).

  PHASE D — Construct THREE regime datasets (this is the 'construct synthetic but realistic traces' step from the direction, applied per regime): (1) Stationary hot clusters — stable Zipf popularity, a few dominant hot clusters; (2) Sudden popularity shift — request mass migrates from old clusters to new ones midway through the sequence; (3) Cold-start — a stream of previously-unseen items with no warm-up. Keep the request sequence ordered with timestamps in each.

  PHASE E — Split by temporal order into train/validation/test (no shuffling across time), write each item as a row {item_id, request_sequence_or_ordered_events, timestamp, embedding (float list), cluster_id, popularity_count, regime, metadata_fold}. Validate against the repo schema with aii-json, and generate full/mini/preview variants. Final output paths: full_*.json, mini_*.json, preview_*.json per regime.

  FAILURE HANDLING: If no real trace is obtainable/loadable, fall back to real-derived popularity params from the documented traces (Phase A records them first) and represent that provenance explicitly in metadata instead of silently synthesizing. If a single 512-d CLIP model is too heavy for CPU, downscale to ViT-B/32 fp16 or a 128-d projection and note it. Do not compute hit/miss or conformal intervals in this artifact.
target_num_datasets: 3
</artifact_plan>

{"content": [{"cache_prompt": false, "type": "text", "text": "**ALWAYS parallelize. Sequential processing is unacceptable for any non-trivial workload.** A sequential script doing 1000 API calls takes hours and fails halfway. An async version finishes in minutes with proper error handling. ALWAYS ask: \"Can this run in parallel?\" \u2014 the answer is almost always yes.\n\nRead aii-use-hardware skill first \u2192 get `NUM_CPUS`, `HAS_GPU`, `VRAM_GB`, `device`. Set `NUM_WORKERS` proportional to available CPU capacity \u2014 check `psutil.cpu_percent(interval=1)` and scale accordingly (e.g. 30% used \u2192 use ~70% of cores).\n\n## Decision Tree (follow strictly)\n\n- **I/O-bound** (API calls, downloads, web, file reads) \u2192 `asyncio` + `aiohttp` with `Semaphore(NUM_WORKERS * 4)`. NEVER do sequential HTTP requests in a loop.\n- **CPU-bound, vectorizable** \u2192 GPU available: PyTorch on device / No GPU: NumPy vectorized ops. NEVER loop over array elements in Python.\n- **CPU-bound, independent items** \u2192 `ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=NUM_WORKERS)`. NEVER process items one-by-one when they're independent.\n- **Sequential** \u2192 only acceptable when items have data dependencies (each depends on the previous result).\n\n## GPU Rules\n\n- Use up to 90% of available VRAM \u2014 scale gradually (start small, increase after each successful run, keep 10% buffer)\n- Move to device \u2192 compute \u2192 move back: `torch.tensor(data, device=device)` \u2192 `.cpu().numpy()`\n- OOM fallback: catch `torch.cuda.OutOfMemoryError` \u2192 `empty_cache()` \u2192 halve batch size \u2192 retry on GPU. Keep reducing until it fits. Stay on GPU.\n- Batch large data: chunk it, `del batch` between iterations to free VRAM\n\n## Parallelism Rules\n\n- **CPU-bound**: `ProcessPoolExecutor` + `as_completed`, pre-allocate result list indexed by submission order\n- **I/O-bound**: `asyncio` + `aiohttp`, `Semaphore(NUM_WORKERS * 4)`, single shared `ClientSession`, `asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True)`\n- Always add `tenacity` retries for transient failures, always set timeouts on HTTP requests\n- **CRITICAL \u2014 `ProcessPoolExecutor` start method**: Default `fork` deadlocks with loguru (and any threading library). ALWAYS pass `mp_context=multiprocessing.get_context(\"spawn\")` when constructing `ProcessPoolExecutor` in any script that uses loguru, threading, or async I/O. Example:\n  ```python\n  import multiprocessing as mp\n  from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor\n  with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=N, mp_context=mp.get_context(\"spawn\")) as pool:\n      ...\n  ```\n\n---\nThis skill is located at `/ai-inventor/.claude/skills/aii-parallel-computing`. Any files it references (e.g. under `scripts/`, `references/`, `assets/`) are relative to that directory."}], "is_error": false, "skill_name": "aii-parallel-computing", "kind": "InvokeSkillObservation"}

{"content": [{"cache_prompt": false, "type": "text", "text": "## Core Principles\n\n1. **Time budget first**: Read your time/runtime constraints before running anything. Set every Bash timeout to fit within the budget.\n2. **Start small, scale up**: Run on minimal input first, fix errors, then increase scale.\n3. **Extrapolate before scaling**: Use recorded runtimes to predict whether the next step fits in the budget. Don't guess \u2014 calculate.\n4. **Background execution**: For anything that takes >1 min, run in background (`run_in_background=true`) and do useful work while waiting.\n5. **Stop early if needed**: Quality results on less data beats a timeout or crash. It's always acceptable to stop at a smaller scale.\n\n---\n\n## Gradual Scaling Sequence\n\nRun code at increasing data sizes, checking runtime at each step.\n\nSubstitute your actual file names:\n- `{mini_file}` \u2014 mini JSON (3 examples) from dependency workspace\n- `{full_file}` \u2014 full dataset from dependency workspace\n- `{script}` \u2014 your processing script (e.g., `./method.py`, `./eval.py`)\n- `{schema}` \u2014 JSON schema to validate output against\n\n**STEP 1 \u2014 MINI DATA:** Run `{script}` on `{mini_file}`. Do NOT truncate logs. Fix all errors. Validate output against `{schema}`. Verify you are NOT using mock scripts, mock data, or mock APIs.\n\n**STEP 2 \u2014 10 EXAMPLES:** Modify `{script}` to load only the first 10 examples from `{full_file}`. Run and fix errors. Validate schema. Record the runtime.\n\n**STEP 3 \u2014 50 EXAMPLES:** Load first 50 examples from `{full_file}`. Run and fix errors. Record runtime. **EXTRAPOLATE**: Using runtimes from steps 2-3, estimate time per example. Calculate how many examples fit in your remaining time budget. If 50 already used most of the budget, stop here.\n\n**STEP 4 \u2014 100 EXAMPLES (if budget allows):** Load first 100 examples. Run and fix errors. Record runtime. Re-extrapolate with the new data point.\n\n**STEP 5 \u2014 200 EXAMPLES (if budget allows):** Load first 200 examples from `{full_file}`. Run and fix errors. Record runtime.\n\n**STEP 6 \u2014 MAXIMIZE:** Using all recorded runtimes, extrapolate time-per-example (it may not be perfectly linear \u2014 account for overhead). Calculate the maximum number of examples that fits within your remaining time budget with a 10% safety margin. Load that many (or all if they fit). Run and validate.\n\n## Final Testing Phase\n\nAfter completing the scaling sequence, redo the entire sequence **one more time** up to your final example count:\n\nmini \u2192 10 \u2192 50 \u2192 100 \u2192 200 \u2192 max\n\nAt each scale: look for issues, fix problems, validate output, ensure it completes within time limits.\n\n---\n\n## Background Execution\n\nFor any step that takes >1 min, run as a **background task**:\n\n1. Launch with Bash `run_in_background=true`\n2. While it runs, use the time productively:\n   - Sanity-check previous outputs\n   - Verify file integrity (correct field names, non-empty values)\n   - Review code for edge cases at larger scale\n   - Prepare the next step\n3. Check back on the background task to get results\n4. If it failed, fix errors and re-run\n\n---\n\n## Resource Limits\n\nSet hard RAM and CPU time limits so code fails fast instead of crashing the system. Read limits from `<hardware>` and leave headroom for the OS (e.g., if 16GB total, cap at 14GB).\n\nPython example using stdlib `resource` module:\n```python\nimport resource\nresource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_AS, (14 * 1024**3, 14 * 1024**3))  # 14GB RAM\nresource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_CPU, (3600, 3600))  # 1 hour CPU time\n```\nExceeding RAM raises `MemoryError`. Exceeding CPU time sends `SIGKILL`.\n\n## Monitoring\n\nAt each step, record runtime AND check resource usage (`free -h` for RAM, `top -bn1 | head -5` for CPU). <artifact_plan>
id: gen_plan_dataset_1_idx2
type: dataset
title: Visual cache access trace dataset
summary: >-
  Build three cache-access trace datasets (stationary hot clusters, popularity shift, cold-start), each pairing a real request
  sequence + per-item popularity with real images and locally-extracted CLIP embeddings, plus per-item cluster/popularity
  metadata, split by temporal order. This supplies the raw inputs the downstream conformal-cache-admission experiment needs
  to replay TinyLFU/ARC2/LRU and the new method.
runpod_compute_profile: cpu_heavy
ideal_dataset_criteria: >-
  The ideal dataset pairs a REAL request trace (item IDs, ordered request sequence, timestamps, per-item request counts showing
  Zipf/heavy-skew popularity) with REAL images so that CLIP embeddings and semantic clusters are genuine and reproducible.
  Concretely: 1,000–20,000 unique items per regime with ~100k–1M total requests; each item carries a 512-d CLIP (ViT-B/32)
  embedding, a semantic cluster id, and its true popularity (request count); PLUS the full ordered request sequence is retained
  (not collapsed to aggregates) so the experiment can replay TinyLFU/ARC2/LRU/bandit/Chameleon policies and compute hit/miss.
  Total footprint under ~300MB. Three regimes with distinct dynamics. Folds split by timestamp (temporal order preserved,
  no future leakage). The dataset must be raw data ONLY: NO hit/miss labels, conformal intervals, or admission decisions should
  be computed here — those are downstream experiment/derived outputs.
dataset_search_plan: |-
  CRITICAL CORRECTION TO THE DIRECTION: (1) OpenRouter does NOT expose CLIP/image-embedding endpoints — it is a text-LLM gateway. Extract embeddings LOCALLY instead using open_clip_torch (ViT-B/32, 512-d) or transformers.CLIPModel on CPU; this also means the $10 OpenRouter budget is not needed for this artifact. (2) Real cache traces (Tencent photo CDN, Microsoft, Wikipedia, SNIA IOTTA block traces) ship item IDs + request sequences + counts but NOT the image bytes, so visual embeddings cannot come from the trace itself — the access pattern and the images must come from two real sources and be paired procedurally.

  PHASE A — Acquire real access-pattern ground truth: Search HuggingFace and GitHub for public cache/CDN trace datasets. Named candidates to check: (a) the Caffeine simulator traces (github.com/ben-manes/caffeine/wiki/Simulator, Traces section) which reference the Tencent photo CDN, Microsoft, Wikipedia, Gloe/S3/UMass traces; (b) the pennshen trace repos on GitHub (LC/CacheLib-traces / PBC) hosting large CDN traces; (c) SNIA IOTTA block-I/O repository (iotta.snia.org). Use aii-hf-datasets search (queries: 'cache trace', 'cdn access log', 'web trace', 'request trace') and aii-web-tools search as fallback. Goal: an ordered request stream + per-item request counts that exhibit heavy-tailed popularity. If no directly loadable trace is found, RECORD the trace's Zipf/skew statistics and request-count distribution and use them as the ground-truth generator for the request sequences (still real-derived, not fabricated ab initio).

  PHASE B — Acquire real images: Use aii-hf-datasets to pull a loadable image corpus — ImageNet-1k subset (via timm/HF mirror) or COCO (e.g. a HF coco/ image subset) is preferred for real semantic clusters (animals, vehicles, food, scenes). Target a few thousand down to 20k images. Confirm 'loadable=True' before choosing.

  PHASE C — Pair and embed: Assign each trace item to a real image deterministically (seeded), cluster items by image class/label into a 'cluster_id' column. Extract 512-d CLIP embeddings locally (CLIP ViT-B/32, CPU-batch, float32→float16 if needed for size).

  PHASE D — Construct THREE regime datasets (this is the 'construct synthetic but realistic traces' step from the direction, applied per regime): (1) Stationary hot clusters — stable Zipf popularity, a few dominant hot clusters; (2) Sudden popularity shift — request mass migrates from old clusters to new ones midway through the sequence; (3) Cold-start — a stream of previously-unseen items with no warm-up. Keep the request sequence ordered with timestamps in each.

  PHASE E — Split by temporal order into train/validation/test (no shuffling across time), write each item as a row {item_id, request_sequence_or_ordered_events, timestamp, embedding (float list), cluster_id, popularity_count, regime, metadata_fold}. Validate against the repo schema with aii-json, and generate full/mini/preview variants. Final output paths: full_*.json, mini_*.json, preview_*.json per regime.

  FAILURE HANDLING: If no real trace is obtainable/loadable, fall back to real-derived popularity params from the documented traces (Phase A records them first) and represent that provenance explicitly in metadata instead of silently synthesizing. If a single 512-d CLIP model is too heavy for CPU, downscale to ViT-B/32 fp16 or a 128-d projection and note it. Do not compute hit/miss or conformal intervals in this artifact.
target_num_datasets: 3
</artifact_plan>

  Total footprint under ~300MB. Three regimes with distinct dynamics. Folds split by timestamp (temporal order preserved,
  no future leakage). The dataset must be raw data ONLY: NO hit/miss labels, conformal intervals, or admission decisions should
  be computed here — those are downstream experiment/derived outputs.
dataset_search_plan: |-
  CRITICAL CORRECTION TO THE DIRECTION: (1) OpenRouter does NOT expose CLIP/image-embedding endpoints — it is a text-LLM gateway. Extract embeddings LOCALLY instead using open_clip_torch (ViT-B/32, 512-d) or transformers.CLIPModel on CPU; this also means the $10 OpenRouter budget is not needed for this artifact. (2) Real cache traces (Tencent photo CDN, Microsoft, Wikipedia, SNIA IOTTA block traces) ship item IDs + request sequences + counts but NOT the image bytes, so visual embeddings cannot come from the trace itself — the access pattern and the images must come from two real sources and be paired procedurally.

  PHASE A — Acquire real access-pattern ground truth: Search HuggingFace and GitHub for public cache/CDN trace datasets. Named candidates to check: (a) the Caffeine simulator traces (github.com/ben-manes/caffeine/wiki/Simulator, Traces section) which reference the Tencent photo CDN, Microsoft, Wikipedia, Gloe/S3/UMass traces; (b) the pennshen trace repos on GitHub (LC/CacheLib-traces / PBC) hosting large CDN traces; (c) SNIA IOTTA block-I/O repository (iotta.snia.org). Use aii-hf-datasets search (queries: 'cache trace', 'cdn access log', 'web trace', 'request trace') and aii-web-tools search as fallback. Goal: an ordered request stream + per-item request counts that exhibit heavy-tailed popularity. If no directly loadable trace is found, RECORD the trace's Zipf/skew statistics and request-count distribution and use them as the ground-truth generator for the request sequences (still real-derived, not fabricated ab initio).

  PHASE B — Acquire real images: Use aii-hf-datasets to pull a loadable image corpus — ImageNet-1k subset (via timm/HF mirror) or COCO (e.g. a HF coco/ image subset) is preferred for real semantic clusters (animals, vehicles, food, scenes). Target a few thousand down to 20k images. Confirm 'loadable=True' before choosing.

  PHASE C — Pair and embed: Assign each trace item to a real image deterministically (seeded), cluster items by image class/label into a 'cluster_id' column. Extract 512-d CLIP embeddings locally (CLIP ViT-B/32, CPU-batch, float32→float16 if needed for size).

  PHASE D — Construct THREE regime datasets (this is the 'construct synthetic but realistic traces' step from the direction, applied per regime): (1) Stationary hot clusters — stable Zipf popularity, a few dominant hot clusters; (2) Sudden popularity shift — request mass migrates from old clusters to new ones midway through the sequence; (3) Cold-start — a stream of previously-unseen items with no warm-up. Keep the request sequence ordered with timestamps in each.

  PHASE E — Split by temporal order into train/validation/test (no shuffling across time), write each item as a row {item_id, request_sequence_or_ordered_events, timestamp, embedding (float list), cluster_id, popularity_count, regime, metadata_fold}. Validate against the repo schema with aii-json, and generate full/mini/preview variants. Final output paths: full_*.json, mini_*.json, preview_*.json per regime.

  FAILURE HANDLING: If no real trace is obtainable/loadable, fall back to real-derived popularity params from the documented traces (Phase A records them first) and represent that provenance explicitly in metadata instead of silently synthesizing. If a single 512-d CLIP model is too heavy for CPU, downscale to ViT-B/32 fp16 or a 128-d projection and note it. Do not compute hit/miss or conformal intervals in this artifact.
target_num_datasets: 3
</artifact_plan>

<artifact_plan>
id: gen_plan_dataset_1_idx2
type: dataset
title: Visual cache access trace dataset
summary: >-
  Build three cache-access trace datasets (stationary hot clusters, popularity shift, cold-start), each pairing a real request
  sequence + per-item popularity with real images and locally-extracted CLIP embeddings, plus per-item cluster/popularity
  metadata, split by temporal order. This supplies the raw inputs the downstream conformal-cache-admission experiment needs
  to replay TinyLFU/ARC2/LRU and the new method.
runpod_compute_profile: cpu_heavy
ideal_dataset_criteria: >-
  The ideal dataset pairs a REAL request trace (item IDs, ordered request sequence, timestamps, per-item request counts showing
  Zipf/heavy-skew popularity) with REAL images so that CLIP embeddings and semantic clusters are genuine and reproducible.
  Concretely: 1,000–20,000 unique items per regime with ~100k–1M total requests; each item carries a 512-d CLIP (ViT-B/32)
  embedding, a semantic cluster id, and its true popularity (request count); PLUS the full ordered request sequence is retained
  (not collapsed to aggregates) so the experiment can replay TinyLFU/ARC2/LRU/bandit/Chameleon policies and compute hit/miss.
  Total footprint under ~300MB. Three regimes with distinct dynamics. Folds split by timestamp (temporal order preserved,
  no future leakage). The dataset must be raw data ONLY: NO hit/miss labels, conformal intervals, or admission decisions should
  be computed here — those are downstream experiment/derived outputs.
dataset_search_plan: |-
  CRITICAL CORRECTION TO THE DIRECTION: (1) OpenRouter does NOT expose CLIP/image-embedding endpoints — it is a text-LLM gateway. Extract embeddings LOCALLY instead using open_clip_torch (ViT-B/32, 512-d) or transformers.CLIPModel on CPU; this also means the $10 OpenRouter budget is not needed for this artifact. (2) Real cache traces (Tencent photo CDN, Microsoft, Wikipedia, SNIA IOTTA block traces) ship item IDs + request sequences + counts but NOT the image bytes, so visual embeddings cannot come from the trace itself — the access pattern and the images must come from two real sources and be paired procedurally.

  PHASE A — Acquire real access-pattern ground truth: Search HuggingFace and GitHub for public cache/CDN trace datasets. Named candidates to check: (a) the Caffeine simulator traces (github.com/ben-manes/caffeine/wiki/Simulator, Traces section) which reference the Tencent photo CDN, Microsoft, Wikipedia, Gloe/S3/UMass traces; (b) the pennshen trace repos on GitHub (LC/CacheLib-traces / PBC) hosting large CDN traces; (c) SNIA IOTTA block-I/O repository (iotta.snia.org). Use aii-hf-datasets search (queries: 'cache trace', 'cdn access log', 'web trace', 'request trace') and aii-web-tools search as fallback. Goal: an ordered request stream + per-item request counts that exhibit heavy-tailed popularity. If no directly loadable trace is found, RECORD the trace's Zipf/skew statistics and request-count distribution and use them as the ground-truth generator for the request sequences (still real-derived, not fabricated ab initio).

  PHASE B — Acquire real images: Use aii-hf-datasets to pull a loadable image corpus — ImageNet-1k subset (via timm/HF mirror) or COCO (e.g. a HF coco/ image subset) is preferred for real semantic clusters (animals, vehicles, food, scenes). Target a few thousand down to 20k images. Confirm 'loadable=True' before choosing.

  PHASE C — Pair and embed: Assign each trace item to a real image deterministically (seeded), cluster items by image class/label into a 'cluster_id' column. Extract 512-d CLIP embeddings locally (CLIP ViT-B/32, CPU-batch, float32→float16 if needed for size).

  PHASE D — Construct THREE regime datasets (this is the 'construct synthetic but realistic traces' step from the direction, applied per regime): (1) Stationary hot clusters — stable Zipf popularity, a few dominant hot clusters; (2) Sudden popularity shift — request mass migrates from old clusters to new ones midway through the sequence; (3) Cold-start — a stream of previously-unseen items with no warm-up. Keep the request sequence ordered with timestamps in each.

  PHASE E — Split by temporal order into train/validation/test (no shuffling across time), write each item as a row {item_id, request_sequence_or_ordered_events, timestamp, embedding (float list), cluster_id, popularity_count, regime, metadata_fold}. Validate against the repo schema with aii-json, and generate full/mini/preview variants. Final output paths: full_*.json, mini_*.json, preview_*.json per regime.

  FAILURE HANDLING: If no real trace is obtainable/loadable, fall back to real-derived popularity params from the documented traces (Phase A records them first) and represent that provenance explicitly in metadata instead of silently synthesizing. If a single 512-d CLIP model is too heavy for CPU, downscale to ViT-B/32 fp16 or a 128-d projection and note it. Do not compute hit/miss or conformal intervals in this artifact.
target_num_datasets: 3
</artifact_plan>

  Zipf/heavy-skew popularity) with REAL images so that CLIP embeddings and semantic clusters are genuine and reproducible.
  Concretely: 1,000–20,000 unique items per regime with ~100k–1M total requests; each item carries a 512-d CLIP (ViT-B/32)
  embedding, a semantic cluster id, and its true popularity (request count); PLUS the full ordered request sequence is retained
  (not collapsed to aggregates) so the experiment can replay TinyLFU/ARC2/LRU/bandit/Chameleon policies and compute hit/miss.

dataset_search_plan: |-
  CRITICAL CORRECTION TO THE DIRECTION: (1) OpenRouter does NOT expose CLIP/image-embedding endpoints — it is a text-LLM gateway. Extract embeddings LOCALLY instead using open_clip_torch (ViT-B/32, 512-d) or transformers.CLIPModel on CPU; this also means the $10 OpenRouter budget is not needed for this artifact. (2) Real cache traces (Tencent photo CDN, Microsoft, Wikipedia, SNIA IOTTA block traces) ship item IDs + request sequences + counts but NOT the image bytes, so visual embeddings cannot come from the trace itself — the access pattern and the images must come from two real sources and be paired procedurally.

  PHASE A — Acquire real access-pattern ground truth: Search HuggingFace and GitHub for public cache/CDN trace datasets. Named candidates to check: (a) the Caffeine simulator traces (github.com/ben-manes/caffeine/wiki/Simulator, Traces section) which reference the Tencent photo CDN, Microsoft, Wikipedia, Gloe/S3/UMass traces; (b) the pennshen trace repos on GitHub (LC/CacheLib-traces / PBC) hosting large CDN traces; (c) SNIA IOTTA block-I/O repository (iotta.snia.org). Use aii-hf-datasets search (queries: 'cache trace', 'cdn access log', 'web trace', 'request trace') and aii-web-tools search as fallback. Goal: an ordered request stream + per-item request counts that exhibit heavy-tailed popularity. If no directly loadable trace is found, RECORD the trace's Zipf/skew statistics and request-count distribution and use them as the ground-truth generator for the request sequences (still real-derived, not fabricated ab initio).

Target a few thousand down to 20k images. Confirm 'loadable=True' before choosing.

  PHASE D — Construct THREE regime datasets (this is the 'construct synthetic but realistic traces' step from the direction, applied per regime): (1) Stationary hot clusters — stable Zipf popularity, a few dominant hot clusters; (2) Sudden popularity shift — request mass migrates from old clusters to new ones midway through the sequence; (3) Cold-start — a stream of previously-unseen items with no warm-up. Keep the request sequence ordered with timestamps in each.
